changes.old: Third-century Antioch was the seedbed of the fourth-century quarrel over the Son. Lucian's pupils led the Arian party, and three of them later taught Aetius, the first Anomoean teacher. Paul's adoptionism and Sabellius' modalism were opposite ways of refusing the account of the Son that the century was working out.

changes.old: In 268 or thereabouts the bishops of Syria and Asia Minor met at Antioch for the third time in a few years to deal with their own metropolitan. Paul of Samosata was bishop of the greatest city in the Roman East. The council that removed him says he liked to be called ducenarius, a salaried official's title, probably held under the Palmyrene rulers of the city. The charges mix doctrine with deportment: that he had a raised throne built for himself in church, that he stopped the old hymns and had new ones sung to himself, that women in his household gave scandal. The teaching at issue was that Christ was a man in whom the Word had come to dwell rather than the Word made flesh - the reading later called adoptionist. The council could not make the deposition stick, because the civil power was Palmyrene and Paul had its favor; he went only when Aurelian retook the city in 272 and settled the question of who owned the church building by asking which claimant was in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome, which is the first time a Roman emperor adjudicated a Christian dispute. The letter announcing the deposition was drafted by Malchion, who ran a rhetorical school in the city and had cross-examined Paul in front of shorthand writers. A generation later, in the same city, a presbyter named Lucian worked over the text of the Greek Bible and taught a circle of students - Arius among them - who afterwards used his name as a badge.

changes.old: Almost everything anyone knows about the first three Christian centuries comes through this library. Eusebius' Church History quotes documents that survive nowhere else, and it was written from shelves Pamphilus and Alexander had assembled - so the shape of early Christian memory is partly the shape of what a Palestinian library happened to hold. The Hexapla, Origen's six-column Old Testament, sat here. Jerome later searched these shelves and treasured copies of Origen made in Pamphilus's own hand. And Africanus' chronicle is the foundation Eusebius built his own chronology on, which in turn became the frame every medieval universal history used.

It was Origen's Old Testament, laid out in six columns. Jerome later searched these shelves. He prized copies of Origen made in Pamphilus's own hand. And Africanus wrote a chronicle. Eusebius built his own timeline on it. That timeline in turn set the frame for each history of the world written in the Middle Ages.

changes.old: Callistus, a former slave once sent to the Sardinian mines, became bishop of Rome. He led his congregation through open arguments over grave sin after baptism, and over speaking of Father and Son without naming two Gods. Hippolytus, a learned presbyter who thought him wrong on every count, set himself up as a rival bishop and wrote a Refutation that, almost by accident, preserves more about second- and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book. Callistus himself left not one word in his own voice.

He also wrote a Refutation. Almost by accident, it preserves more about second- and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book. Callistus himself left not one word in his own voice.

changes.old: The questions argued here did not go away. After the persecution of 250, Rome had to decide whether Christians who had sacrificed could be restored. The quarrel split the city in the Novatian schism of 251. Rome's answer - that they could - is the one the Western church kept. Hippolytus' Refutation, written to discredit Callistus, incidentally preserves more information about second and third-century religious movements than any other surviving book.

changes.old: Victorinus' recapitulation reading of the Apocalypse - that the seals, trumpets and bowls narrate the same events over again rather than a sequence of them - survived Jerome's revision. Tyconius and Augustine also taught readers to watch for recapitulation, though neither names Victorinus. It became the standard Western reading of the book. That is a long career for a commentary its own editor thought needed fixing. The millenarianism did not survive the same journey, which is roughly the point: what the Latin West kept of its first exegete is what its second exegete was willing to pass on.
changes.new: Victorinus read the Apocalypse as recapitulation. On this reading, the seals, trumpets and bowls tell the same events over again, not a sequence of them. That is a long career for a commentary that its own editor thought needed fixing. The millenarianism did not make the same journey. That is roughly the point. What the Latin West kept of its first interpreter of scripture is what its second was willing to pass on.

changes.old: Bardaisan of Edessa was a courtier, an archer of some reputation, a philosopher, and by his own lights a Christian. He wrote against Marcion, and he was baptized in the Edessene church. He and his school made hymns that Ephraim later accused of sweetening poison for the simple, and Ephraim answered them with hymns of his own. What he actually taught is hard to recover. The Book of the Laws of Countries, written by his pupil Philip, presents him arguing that human freedom is real against the fatalism of the astrologers, which is a thoroughly Christian argument. Ephraim, writing a century and a half later in the same city, presents him as a heretic with a cosmology of primordial beings and a defective doctrine of the body's resurrection. Both cannot be the whole truth, and the sources that would settle it are gone.
